+1/+1 counter.intro: +1/+1 counters are the most common type of counter in Magic, with 2,964 cards that use them. +1/+1 counters were introduced in Alpha.
+1/+1 counter.description:
A +1/+1 counter on a creature adds one to its power and toughness. Creatures using +1/+1 counters were among the most popular in the early history of the game.

Charge counters serve as the equivalent default counter for noncreature permanents.

Any color can put +1/+1 counters on themselves, but white and green are best overall at doing it including putting them on other creatures. The creations of, and caring about, +1/+1 counters are secondary in black, and tertiary in blue and red.

−1/−1 counter.intro: −1/−1 counters are the third most common counter type in Magic, with 243 cards, following loyalty counters at 340 cards. They were introduced on the Arabian Nights card Unstable Mutation, and were used as major set themes in Shadowmoor and Eventide, Scars of Mirrodin block, Amonkhet block, and Lorwyn Eclipsed.
−1/−1 counter.description:
−1/−1 counters appear in all five colors but are primarily in black. Flavorwise, putting −1/−1 counters on a creature usually indicates a character being scarred or infected. Shadowmoor's design used replacement effects to signify "damaged" creatures, with a few ways to remove counters flavored as "healing" effects. Scars of Mirrodin used them aggressively on opponent's creatures as "infection", which grew worse with the effect of proliferate.

For ease of comprehension, blocks tend to focus on only a single type of counter on creatures. −1/−1 counters are used less often than +1/+1 counters because they have less available design space, due to their similarity to +1/+1 counters and their capacity to kill creatures and hence a finite number of counters can be present on any given board state. R&D considers them not conducive to making dynamic play environments. −1/−1 counters are currently ranked at a 5 on the Storm Scale for individual cards, and a 7 for use as one of the main mechanics of a set.

As a further concession to mitigate complexity, +1/+1 counters and −1/−1 counters are the only power/toughness altering counters used in new products. Additionally, they are never used as a major component in the same set, to minimize confusion in limited play, unless the product is for more experienced players, such as for the Modern Horizons series. This was relaxed by proxy for Massacre Girl, Known Killer in Murders at Karlov Manor, which uses wither, and more directly for Duskmourn: House of Horror on Patched Plaything. A small handful of cards from the earliest sets still use other, obsolete counters, which may have partial negative numbers.

Acorn counter.intro: Acorn counters are a type of resource counter that may be placed on either a player or a permanent depending on its usage.
Acorn counter.description:
The silver-bordered Acornelia, Fashionable Filcher from Unsanctioned was the first card to feature Acorn counters. They have their own symbol , and may be used as a resource. They are placed on players rather than on objects. Because of this, they are similar to energy counters.

Chitterspitter from Modern Horizons 2 is the first black-border card and first artifact to use acorn counters. It doesn't use the acorn holofoil stamp. Unlike with the previous usage, Chitterspitter places the counters on itself. Acorn counters on a permanent cannot be used for Acornelia so the two types do not interact.

With the release of Alchemy: Bloomburrow, acorn counters returned in the form of Euru, Acorn Scrounger. Euru is tied to the Chitterspitter, allowing additional acorn counters to be placed on it.

Aegis counter.intro: Aegis counters are a type of counter that may be placed on a creature to temporarily Exile it.
Aegis counter.description: Livio, Oathsworn Sentinel from Commander Legends is the first card to use Aegis counters. The counters are placed on a creature as its owner Exiles it and then allows for it to be returned to the Battlefield under its owner's control. This acts as temporary protection for the creature.

Age counter.intro: Age counters are usually placed during the upkeep step. They are exclusively used by cards with cumulative upkeep.

Aim counter.intro: Aim counters are a type of counter that represent a ranged attack.
Aim counter.description:
Hankyu from Champions of Kamigawa is the first artifact equipment to use aim counters. They are placed on the equipment and allow the creature that equipped them to deal damage per counter to another creature representing attacking with a bow and arrow.

Haphazard Bombardment from Dominaria is the first enchantment to use aim counters. It represents targets placed on a permanent marking for potential destruction.

Arrow counter.intro: Arrow counters are a type of counter on one of Urza's growing enchantments.
Arrow counter.description: Archery Training from Urza's Destiny is the only card to use arrow counters. They grant the enchanted creature an ability to deal damage to a creature in combat per arrow counter on the enchantment.

Arrowhead counter.intro: Arrowhead counters are a type of counter that weakens creatures by creating −1/−1 counters.
Arrowhead counter.description: Serrated Arrows from Homelands is the only card to use arrowhead counters. It uses these counters to store the number of −1/−1 counters that it could put on a target creature.

Awakening counter.intro: Awakening counters are a type of counter that is placed on Lands which makes them a Land creature.
Awakening counter.description: Liege of the Tangle from Scars of Mirrodin is the first creature to produce awakening counters. The counters are placed on any number of lands under the player's control whenever the creature deals damage. Any land that has an Awakening counter becomes a Green Elemental Land creature. This represents the awakening of the land into Elementals.

Bait counter.intro: Bait counters are a type of counter introduced in Magic: The Gathering Foundations.
Bait counter.description: Bait counters were introduced on Fishing Pole as a thematic way of representing a creature fishing. Fishing Pole is an equipment that gives a creature the activated ability which can be used to add a bait counter to the Pole for one colorless mana. Whenever the equipped creature becomes untapped, one of the bait counter is removed from the Fishing Pole to create a 1/1 blue Fish token. This represents the bait on the pole catching a fish.

Blaze counter.intro: Blaze counters are a type of counter that deals damage based on different conditions representing fire.
Blaze counter.description:
Obsidian Fireheart from Zendikar is the first creature to produce blaze counters. The counters are placed on lands by the Elemental via an Activated ability. Lands with the counters deal damage to their controlling player at the beginning of their upkeep. This represents the land is on fire. The counters continue existing on the lands even after the creature that spawned them is gone from the battlefield. The counter being moved from the land causes the damage to cease and does not transfer the ability to another land even if the counter is on it. The ability only works when the counter is placed by the elemental. Multiple blaze counters also do not increase the damage.

Five-Alarm Fire from Gatecrash is the first enchantment to produce blaze counters. In this case, the counters are placed on the Enchantment itself whenever a creature under the player's control deals damage. They act as a resource for an ability to deal 5 damage to a creature or player consuming 5 counters on it per use.

Blessing counter.intro: Blessing counters are a type of counter introduced in the Commander Masters Enduring Enchantments commander deck.
Blessing counter.description: Blessing counters first appeared on Boon of the Spirit Realm, where they represent the strength offered by the kami.

Blight counter.intro: Blight counters are a type of counter introduced in Bloomburrow.
Blight counter.description:
At is introduction, Blight counters represented the expanding of trail of death left by the Rottenmouth Viper, a Calamity Beast from Bloomburrow. Whenever the Viper enters or attacks, one of the counters is added to it and then for each counter on it, the controller's opponents must lose 4 life unless they sacrifice a nonland permanent or discard a card.

Final Fantasy added Ultima, Origin of Oblivion which uses these counters similar to Flood counters, but transforming lands into Wastes instead.

Blood counter.intro: Blood counters are a type of counter introduced in the Ravnica block that act as resources for activated abilities. They usually involve an exchange or sacrifice to be created after which they can be used as a resource on activated abilities.
Blood counter.description:
Blood counters first appeared on two artifacts in the Ravnica block. Bloodletter Quill from Ravnica: City of Guilds is the first card and artifact to use blood counters. Blood counters build up on the artifact per use of its ability and cause damage to the player unless removed via another activated ability. Rakdos Riteknife from Dissension also used blood counters as an equipment. Blood counters could be created on it by sacrificing creatures. The owner could then force a player to sacrifice a permanent per counter on the equipment if they sacrificed it. Ravnica Allegiance re-introduced Blood counters on the Font of Agonies enchantment which spawns blood counters whenever the player pays life allowing them to be later used to destroy creatures.

Commander 2019 was the first non-Ravnica set to use Blood counters. Unlike the other uses, in this case a Legendary Vampire creature - Rayami, First of the Fallen - both exiles any creature that dies and places a blood cocunter on them. Rayami then gains up to 13 possible keyword abilities if any of the exiled creatures with a blood counter has those abilities.

Bloodline counter.intro: Bloodline counters are a type of counter that tracks upkeep and the trigger for the Transform mechanic of Double-faced cards.
Bloodline counter.description: Bloodline counters were introduced in Innistrad: Crimson Vow on the artifact known as Edgar Markov's Coffin. A counter is placed on the artifact after the player’s upkeep along with creating a vampire token. Once three or more of the counters are on the coffin, it transforms as a Double-faced card into Edgar, Charmed Groom. This represents Edgar Markov’s vampire bloodline and his revival from the coffin after a period of sleep.
Bloodline counter.use: Counter for Double-faced card‘s transform trigger

Bloodstain counter.intro: Bloodstain counters are a type of counter introduced in Murders at Karlov Manor.
Bloodstain counter.description: Bloodstain counters are used as a thematic representation of a crime scene and how that case is solved by the Ravnican Agency of Magicological Investigations. Creatures dying increase the amount of counters on the card alongside requiring a mill which represents more evidence being found. Once enough evidence is analyzed which is five or more of the counters, Blood Spatter Analysis is sacrificed and allows the return a creature from a graveyard to the player's hand.
Bloodstain counter.use: Tracking the number of creatures that have died

Book counter.intro: Book counters are a type of counter introduced in Strixhaven: School of Mages that act as resources for activated abilities. They are created via the Magecraft mechanic which means a counter is created whenever an instant or sorcery spell is cast.
Book counter.description: Book counters first appeared on an artifact in Strixhaven. Spell Satchel is the first card and artifact to use book counters. Book counters build up on the artifact whenever the player casts an instant or sorcery alluding to the artifact gaining energy from each spell cast. It then has activated abilities to either convert a book counter into one Colorless mana or multiple into a card draw. One of its abilities was rebalanced in Magic: The Gathering Arena on April 7, 2022, to allow for easier use and scaling by making it so only 2 book counters equaled a card draw rather than the 3 initially printed on the card.

Bounty counter.intro: Bounty counters are a type of counter introduced in Tempest that originally marked creatures for future destruction but later expanded to mark them so that the player got rewards on their death.
Bounty counter.description:
Bounty counters first appeared on the Bounty Hunter card in Tempest. It has an activated ability that places one of the counters on a non-black creature which marked it for another ability that could destroy the creature. The initial usage seemed analogous to putting a bounty on the given creature for its death while subsequent uses acted as fulfilling the bounty and getting a reward of life and card draws for the creature's death.

The first card to use the second type of bounty counter was Mathas, Fiend Seeker in Commander 2017. It marked an opponent's creature each turn with a counter which made it so opposing players gained 2 life and a card draw on the creature's death. Chevill, Bane of Monsters from Ikoria: Lair of Behemoths had a similar use for them but expanded their placement to include an opponent's planeswalker cards. It adds a bounty counter to an opponent's creature or planeswalker if none had bounty counters on them already. Then once that permanent dies, it gives the player 3 life and a card draw.

Use of the first type of bounty counter returned in Jumpstart 2022 with Termination Facilitator. It has an activated ability that places one of the counters on a creature or planeswalker which marks it for its second ability. Unlike Bounty Hunter, its second ability allows any source of damage to destroy the marked creature. Bounty counters were also used by the Bounty Board in Thunder Junction Commander.
Bounty counter.use: Marker for creature's death or reward on its death

Brain counter.intro: A brain counter is a counter introduced as part of Universes Beyond: Fallout.
Brain counter.description: Brain counters are used by Rex, Cyber-Hound to gain the activated abilities of creature cards exiled with it.

Bribery counter.intro: Bribery counters are a type of counter introduced in Conflux and later reprinted in Commander 2016 and Battlebond. Creatures with the counters on them aren't able to attack or block.
Bribery counter.description:
Bribery counters first appeared on Gwafa Hazid, Profiteer in Conflux. It has an activated ability that places bribery counters on a creature while giving its owner a card. It then prevents the creature marked by the counter from attacking or blocking. This alludes to the creature being bribed to ignore the opponent.

The effect of the counter remains active as long as the placing card remains on the battlefield. The effect goes away if the placing creature is removed from the battlefield but the counters remain where they are. If another of the placing creature enters the battlefield, the creatures with the old counters become affected and once again lose their ability to attack or block.
Bribery counter.use: Prevents creatures from attacking or blocking

Brick counter.intro: Brick counters are a type of counter introduced in Amonkhet. They are created by and placed on a cycle of artifacts known as monuments that were made to represent the constant monument-building that went on in ancient Egypt. They act as a resource, granting the artifact a stronger ability after it builds up the counters via using its weaker ability. They were represented on punch cards in the Amonkhet block.
Brick counter.description:
Brick counters first appeared on a cycle of four artifacts in Amonkhet known as monuments. Each monument is an artifact with two tap abilities, one of which has a minor effect and adds brick counters, and the other is a more powerful version that requires having three brick counters to activate:

Edifice of Authority can prevent a creature from attacking for a turn. The upgraded ability will prevent a creature from attacking, blocking, or using abilities for a turn. Both cost Luxa River Shrine gains one life for , while the upgraded ability gains two life for no mana. Oracle's Vault has the ability to exile the top card of the player's library for , allowing them to play it during that turn. The upgraded ability costs zero and the card can be cast without paying its mana cost. Pyramid of the Pantheon filters into any colored mana. The upgraded ability creates three mana of one color.

Hour of Devastation introduced Sunset Pyramid as a fifth monument that uses brick counters. Both tap abilities cost to activate. Instead of generating counters with its ability, it enters with three counters and removes them to draw a card. Once depleted, the downgraded ability is to Scry 1.

Burden counter.intro: Burden counters are a type of counter introduced in The Lord of the Rings: Tales of Middle-Earth.
Burden counter.description: Burden counters first appeared on The One Ring, where they represent the corrupting nature of the ring in the lore; as the longer one held it, the further and more it would corrupt them.
Burden counter.use: Upkeep tracking for corruption to the One Ring

Cage counter.intro: Cage counters are a type of counter introduced in Commander 2017. They are placed on exiled creatures and artifacts, allowing another card to gain their activated abilities.
Cage counter.description:
Cage counters first appeared on Mairsil, the Pretender in Commander 2017. When it first enters the battlefield, it exiles an artifact or creature with a Cage counter on it. It then gains the activated abilities of the card with the Cage counter, allowing one use per turn. The name of the counter alludes to the exiled card being caged.

The effect of copying the activated abilities of any card with the Cage counters caused many rule clarifications, with a total of 11 different notes on the Gatherer regarding how various types of copied activated abilities are copied. Examples include being able to copy a crew ability but not an equip ability, how linked activated abilities are copied, and how multiple of the same ability can be copied.

The counter was featured again on a 2024 Unknown Event playtest card Seer of the Bright Side, which was a human assassin that enters with two of the counters on it. They have a differently flavored effect in this use, where they represent the Seer being caged and then unleashed by preventing it from attacking or blocking while the counters are on it.
Cage counter.use: Copies the abilities of an exiled artifact or creature

Carrion counter.intro: Carrion counters are a type of counter introduced in Legends and later reprinted in Fourth Edition, Renaissance, and most recently Masters Edition IV. Its name alludes to the creature powering up from eating a dead creature as they act as a resource created from creature deaths and can be converted to temporary +1/+1 counters.
Carrion counter.description: Carrion counters first appeared on Osai Vultures in Legends as an unnamed counter on the printed card but was later errated to be typed as Carrion counters. A Carrion counter is created on the creature at the end of a player's turn if another creature was put into the graveyard that turn. Two carrion counters can then be converted into a +1/+1 counter that lasts for a single turn.
Carrion counter.use: Resource for temporary +1/+1 counters created from creatures entering the graveyard

Cell counter.intro: Cell counters are a type of counter introduced in the Final Fantasy commander deck Limit Break. They are placed on creatures, making them modified. They have no other inherent rules.
Cell counter.description:
Cell counters first appeared on Sephiroth, Fallen Hero in the Limit Break commander deck.

Cell counters are flavored as the cells of Jenova, an ancient alien and major antagonist of the Final Fantasy VII series. They serve as a central plot point for the series' story and the primary crisis of Final Fantasy VII. Jenova cells were used by the Shinra Electric Power Company to genetically modify humans in a misguided attempt to create a human-Cetra hybrid that would allow the company to find the "Promised Land" and the untold riches within. The Jenova Project resulted in significantly enhanced individuals used as solders by the company. It was this project that created Sephiroth and permanently altered Cloud Strife.

Charge counter.intro: Charge counters are the default counter for noncreature permanents, and are used most often on artifacts. They are the fourth most common counter in Magic at 152 cards, following -1/-1 counters at 243. They are used for tracking the sunburst and station mechanics.
Charge counter.description:
Some keyword mechanics use charge counters, and some cards interact with charge counters specifically. They are one of the few counter types that exist for reasons other than flavor. Charge counters are deciduous.

In Magic Online, the counter is colored green because it is generally a positive effect. The charge counter shares its icon with Crystal and Gem counters.

Coin counter.intro: Coin counters are a type of counter introduced in Theros: Beyond Death placed on creatures to thematically represent the Ancient Greek practice of placing coins in with the deceased for payment to be carried to the afterlife. In a later set, they had a different distinct usage on artifacts allowing for exchange into Treasure tokens.
Coin counter.description:
Coin counters first appeared on Athreos, Shroud-Veiled in Theros: Beyond Death. They were placed on a creature at the end of the Player's turn giving it the effect of returning to the battlefield under the player's control whenever it died or was exiled in exchange for the coin counter. This represents the God bringing the creature back to life under its control. Thus it acts as either protection for creatures on its side or a way to steal an enemy's creatures upon their death.

Coin counters later appeared again on Noble's Purse in Commander Legends: Battle for Baldur's Gate though in this case they were placed on the artifact and behaved differently. The artifact started with 3 coin counters and could exchange one for creating a Treasure token that could be sacrificed for mana. This acted as if the coins are being used to buy a treasure.

While the use of coin counters on creatures seems to be unrelated to their use on artifacts the two can affect each other. Multiple effects can cause artifacts like Noble's Purse to become creatures, which would allow Athreos to "steal" such an artifact if it were destroyed with coin counters on it. Athreos could also supply extra coin counters to such an artifact beyond its initial supply.
Coin counter.use: Returns creature from death or exile under Player's control; Resource for Treasure tokens.

Collection counter.intro: Collection counter are a type of counter introduced in Streets of New Capenna. Its name alludes to having a collection of cards in exile for later use.
Collection counter.description:
Collection counters first appeared on Evelyn, the Covetous in Streets of New Capenna, where they tracked cards exiled form the top of each player's library whenever a Vampire enters the battlefield. The player in control of Evelyn is then able to cast one of the exiled cards per turn while using mana of any color for their casting cost.

When the counters returned in Modern Horizons 3, they were used to represent the Charitable Levy collecting payments from players.

Component counter.intro: Component counter are a type of counter introduced in Forgotten Realms Commander as a reference to the Dungeons & Dragons concept of a component pouch that spellcasters kept their components or foci for spell casting.
Component counter.description: Component counters first appeared on Component Pouch in Forgotten Realms Commander. It had an activated ability that made use of dice rolling to either add 1 or 2 component counters on the artifact. Each component counter could then be converted to two mana of different colors via another activated ability.

Contested counter.intro: Contested counter are a type of counter introduced in New Capenna Commander that allow for the change of ownership of lands among the players whenever one is dealt damage.
Contested counter.description: Contested counters first appeared on Turf War in New Capenna Commander. This enchantment adds a contested counter on one land controlled by each player. Then, if a creature deals combat damage to a player who controls a land(s) with contested counters, the attacking creature's controller can steal one of those lands. These counters simulate gang fighting over a given piece of land and allow for them to shift control throughout the game whenever a player is damaged.
Contested counter.use: Land Stealing on Damage to Player

Corruption counter.intro: Corruption counters are a type of counter introduced in Modern Horizons 2 currently specific to the planeswalker Geyadrone Dihada.
Corruption counter.description: Corruption counters first appeared on Geyadrone Dihada in Modern Horizons 2. The planeswalker has a base loyalty ability to add a corruption counter on a creature or planeswalker while also having protection against any permanent with one of the counters. Its other abilities then also allow it to take control of permanents, one lesser ability to do so for a turn while also adding a corruption counter to it and the main ability to gain complete control of a permanent with the counter.
Corruption counter.use: Marks for protection and control stealing

CRANK! counter.intro: The CRANK! counter is a counter introduced in Unstable. The CRANK! counter is exclusively connected to Contraption cards. It is used to track which sprocket is active, and thus, which Contraptions can be cranked each turn. At the beginning of each upkeep, it is placed onto the next sprocket. If you don't have any Contraptions on the battlefield, then you don't need to move the CRANK! counter.

Credit counter.intro: Credit counters are a type of counter introduced in Fallen Empires. They are a type of upkeep tracking counter that can be used to gain life.
Credit counter.description: Credit counters first appeared on Icatian Moneychanger in Fallen Empires. The card initially gets 3 Credit counters in exchange for dealing 3 damage to the player. This acts as the initial Credit or loan of life. It will then gain an additional counter every turn on the player's upkeep which acts as the interest on the credit. The creature can then be sacrificed allowing for the player to gain life equal to the number of credit counters on it which acts as cashing in the credit or loan.

Croak counter.intro: Croak counters are a type of counter introduced in Innistrad: Crimson Vow. They are a type of counter that grants the ability to play lands or cast spells from Exile.
Croak counter.description: Croak counters first appeared on Grolnok, the Omnivore in Innistrad: Crimson Vow. The card can mill 3 cards whenever a Frog the player controls attacks but instead of being put in the graveyard, the cards are instead exiled with Croak counters on them. The player is then able to play any lands or cast spells from among those exiled with Croak counters.
Croak counter.use: Play Lands and Cast Spells from Exile

Corpse counter.intro: Corpse counters are a type of counter introduced in Alpha. All instances of corpse counters are created from Black cards and their creation is either related to a creature dying during a given turn or related to tracking a creature that returned from the graveyard. The counters are then used for various effects ranging from token creation, regeneration, or tracking whether a creature should be exiled upon death.
Corpse counter.description:
Corpse counters first appeared on Scavenging Ghoul in Alpha as an unnamed counter which was later errated to be a corpse counter. At the end of each turn, the Ghoul would gain a corpse counter for each creature that died that turn. It could then exchange a corpse counter to regenerate itself.

Corpse counters were seen once again in Core Set 2019 on Isareth the Awakener. It can return creatures from the graveyard with corpse counters on them which are then exiled if they go anywhere other than exile. From the Catacombs, a sorcery from Commander Legends: Battle for Baldur's Gate does the same thing. In these cases, the corpse counter is intended simply as reminder: The exile effect of Isareth or Catacombs will still take place even if the reanimated card has had its corpse counter removed from it, and will not take place on a card which acquired the corpse counter by other means, such as The Ozolith. However, if a corpse counter is put on Scavenging Ghoul by either Isareth or Catacombs, that counter could be used to regenerate the Ghoul, just like its other corpse counters.

The Crowded Crypt artifact from Midnight Hunt Commander saw the third type of corpse counter. This type is generated similarly to the Ghoul's, building up whenever a creature under the control of the player dies. Its use is very different: the Crypt can sacrifice itself to create zombie tokens for each corpse counter on it.

Thus far, all instances of corpse counters do not typically interact with each other, though there are sideways methods to exploit them, by either transferring counters among permanents, or using Isareth the Awakener or From the Catacombs directly on a Scavenging Ghoul to give it an extra corpse counter.

Crystal counter.intro: Crystal counters are a type of counter introduced in Battle for Zendikar. They are a type of counter created by the Converge mechanic and then used as a resource for an activated ability.
Crystal counter.description: Crystal counters first appeared on Prism Array in Battle for Zendikar. They are created on the Enchantment by the Converge mechanic meaning one is added to it per each color of mana spent on the spell. The Crystal counters can then be used as as a resource and exchanged to tap a creature per counter.

Cube counter.intro: Cube counter are a type of counter introduced in Fallen Empires. They act as a resource for regenerating creatures.
Cube counter.description: Cube counters first appeared on Delif's Cube in Fallen Empires. It is an artifact with an ability that when activated will cause a creature the player controls to deal no combat damage on a successful attack in exchange for creating a cube counter on the artifact. The Cube counter can then be exchanged for regenerating a target creature via another activated ability.

Currency counter.intro: Currency counters are a type of counter introduced in Homelands.
Currency counter.description: Currency counters first appeared on Trade Caravan in Homelands. They represent the currency the trade caravan takes in and act as an upkeep tracking counter, which builds up a resource for an activated ability. The Trade Caravan gains a currency counter on each upkeep and then has the activated ability to remove two of the counters in exchange for untapping a land during the opponent's upkeep step.
Currency counter.use: Upkeep tracking; Resource for untapping land

Death counter.intro: Death counters are a type of counter introduced in Visions. It acts as a tracker for sending a creature into Exile when it dies.
Death counter.description:
Death counters first appeared on Bogardan Phoenix in Visions. It is a creature with an ability that returns it to the battlefield on its death with a Death counter. Then when it dies again with the counter on it, it is exiled instead. Their usage in this case represents the power of a phoenix to reincarnate itself on its death.

Death counters are nearly identical in functionality to finality counters, except that they exile from the graveyard rather than creating a replacement effect.

Defense counter.intro: Defense counters are counters that are used to track the defense of battles. They were introduced in March of the Machine.
Defense counter.description: Defense counters are exclusively connected to battle cards and represent how much damage attacking players need to win the battle. Battles enter play with the number of defense counters printed on their card. They lose defense counters corresponding to damage dealt to them.

Delay counter.intro: Delay counters are a type of counter introduced in Tempest. Both instances of it are used to delay effects to a later turn's upkeep.
Delay counter.description:
Delay counters first appeared in Tempest on Ertai's Meddling. It was an instant that allowed for the exile of a spell with delay counters equal to the number of additional mana used to cast. A counter is removed at each upkeep and a copy of the spell returns to the stack once all delay counters are removed from it.

They appeared once again on Delaying Shield in Odyssey. In this case it was an enchantment which would convert damage done to the player into Delay counters on it instead. Then at the beginning of upkeep the delay counters are removed and the player would take damage for each one unless they pay some mana to counteract it.

The different types of Delay counters do not currently interact.

Depletion counter.intro: Depletion counters are used by two very different cycles of lands to limit the activation of their better abilities.

Descent counter.intro: Descent counters are a type of counter introduced in Commander Legends: Battle for Baldur's Gate. They represent an increasing effect each turn due to a thematic descent.
Descent counter.description: Descent counters first appeared on Descent into Avernus in Commander Legends: Battle for Baldur's Gate. Each turn 2 of the counters are added to the enchantment and then each player gets Treasure tokens equal to the number of counters on it as well as takes that amount of damage as well. The counters represent the increasing danger of traveling into Avernus but also the increasing reward in the form of Treasure.
Descent counter.use: Upkeep tracking; Increasing effect each turn due to a thematic descent

Despair counter.intro: Despair counters are a type of counter introduced in Avacyn Restored. They act as an upkeep tracker for an exile effect for each player.
Despair counter.description: Despair counters first appeared on Descent into Madness in Avacyn Restored. Each turn at the player's upkeep a counter is added to the enchantment which then causes each player to exile a permanent they control or a card in their hand for the number of counters on it. This represents increasing despair for the player as they descend into further madness from the enchantment.
Despair counter.use: Upkeep tracking; Exile permanent or card in hand each turn

Devotion counter.intro: Devotion counters are a type of counter introduced in Champions of Kamigawa. They gave bonus effects when another creature or creature type was in play representing a creature's devotion to another.
Devotion counter.description: Devotion counters first appeared on Pious Kitsune and Bloodthirsty Ogre in Champions of Kamigawa. For Pious Kitsune they are created on each upkeep and act as a resource for an ability that gives life. They also have an additional effect representing the 'devotion' aspect of the counter in that if Eight-and-a-Half-Tails is in play then each upkeep the player gains life for each counter. For Bloodthirsty Ogre, it has an activated ability to create the devotion counts while another gives a creature −1/−1 until the end of the turn but only if the player controls a Demon. This acts as the creature's devotion to demons.
Devotion counter.use: Effect while another creature is in play

Discovery counter.intro: Discovery counters are a type of counter introduced in the Universes Beyond Tomb Raider drop of Secret Lair Drop Series: Secretversary 2023.
Discovery counter.description: Discovery counters first appeared on Lara Croft, Tomb Raider. They represent lost treasures, hidden in ruins and tombs (represented by exile) and Lara finding them on her expeditions and adventures. Whenever Lara Croft attacks, up to one target legendary artifact card or legendary land card is exiled from a graveyard and with a discovery counter on it. The controlling player may play a card from exile with a discovery counter on it in the same turn.

Divinity counter.intro: Divinity counters, while having no inherent rules meaning, are consistently and exclusively used by an unnamed mechanic to grant permanents indestructible. Because they are not defined as doing so in the Comprehensive Rules, they only grant indestructible so long as a permanent with such an ability is on the battlefield.
Divinity counter.description:
Divinity counters first appeared on Champions of Kamigawa's myojin cycle: Myojin of Cleansing Fire, Myojin of Infinite Rage, Myojin of Life's Web, Myojin of Night's Reach, and Myojin of Seeing Winds. While the myojin were initially designed as indestructible at all times, there was concern that they would be too powerful in reanimator decks. For that reason, they were changed to rely on divinity counters for indestructible and only acquired divinity counters when cast from the hand. They are also used by That Which Was Taken from Betrayers of Kamigawa, which can add divinity counters and grant indestructible to any permanent.

They reappeared on Bant in Planechase and Kindred Boon in Commander 2017. With keyword counters introduced in Ikoria: Lair of Behemoths, divinity counters were largely supplanted by indestructible counters - and in Kamigawa: Neon Dynasty, a new cycle of Myojins were printed to highlight this fact.

Doom counter.intro: Doom counters are a type of counter introduced in Antiquities. They act as markers for various forms of future thematic doom, some sort of damage or destruction to players or permanents.
Doom counter.description:
Despair counters first appeared on Armageddon Clock in Antiquities as unnamed counters which were later given errata to be Doom counters. It was an artifact that would build up a Doom counter each upkeep and then deal damage to each player equal to the number of counters on it during each draw step. Each player could also activate its ability to remove a Doom counter for a mana cost.

The counters appeared once again on Eye of Doom in Commander 2013. It is an artifact that allows each player to place a Doom counter on a non-land permanent when it enters the battlefield. It can then be sacrificed to destroy all permanents with a Doom counter on them.

Hour of Devastation also saw the return of Doom counters with Imminent Doom which was an enchantment that enters the battlefield with one on it. It would then deal damage to an opponent whenever the player plays a spell with a mana cost equal to the number of Doom counters alongside gaining another.

The counter appeared in Commander 2020 on Lavabrink Floodgates which gave the choice of adding or removing a Doom counter each upkeep. If it builds up to 3 Doom counters then the artifact is sacrificed and deals 6 damage to each creature.
Doom counter.use: Marker for future thematic doom causing damage or destruction to players or permanents

Dream counter.intro: Dream counters are a type of counter introduced in Legends. They have currently always been a resource associated with Rasputin Dreamweaver.
Dream counter.description: Dream counters first appeared on Rasputin Dreamweaver in Legends. He enters the battlefield with 7 Dream counters and can gain another during Upkeep if he is untapped and has less than 7. The counters can then be used to give colorless mana or prevent a point of damage. The counters made a re-appearance in Dominaria United Commander on Rasputin, the Oneiromancer. In this case, he gets a dream counter for each opponent the player has. They can then be used for an activated ability to create colorless mana or a 2/2 white Knight creature token with protection from red.

Duty counter.intro: Duty counters are a type of counter introduced in the Murders at Karlov Manor Commander decks.
Duty counter.description: Duty counters first appeared on Immortal Obligation, referencing the Orzhov Syndicate raising and conscripting spirits, and how even after death, your debt is still due. It returns a creature from an opponents graveyard under their control but with one of the counters on it. For as long as the creature has that counter, it makes the them goaded and doesn’t allow the creature to attack or defend the placing player or their permanents. This essentially forces the opponent to attack other players in a Commander game while making the placing player mostly immune to it. These effects reference the creatures debt to the player for brining it back to life.
Duty counter.use: Marker for an opponent’s creature being goaded, can’t attack or block placing player or their permenants

Echo counter.intro: Echo counters are a type of counter introduced in Mirage. They are used as a marker for an ability that allows them to essentially take the place of 1 damage that would have been dealt to a player.
Echo counter.description: Echo counters first appeared on Soul Echo in Mirage. It is an enchantment that enters the battlefield with Echo counters equal to its additional mana cost. The enchantment makes it so the player does not lose the game for having 0 life and allows for an opponent to choose to remove a counter from it in place of dealing 1 damage to the player. The counters represent an echo of the player that absorbs some damage being dealt against them.
Echo counter.use: Takes place of 1 damage to a player

Egg counter.intro: Egg counters are a type of counter introduced in Dominaria. They have been used to represent some form of birth or rebirth of a creature.
Egg counter.description:
Egg counters first appeared on Darigaaz Reincarnated in Dominaria. They are created on the creature when it dies and is exiled per its ability. The counters then act as an upkeep tracker with one being removed each turn allowing the creature to return to the battlefield once they are all removed. In this instance, the counters are used to represent Darigaaz's ability to reincarnate.

The counters appeared again with a different effect on Xira, the Golden Sting in Dominaria United Commander Decks. In this case, an egg counter is put on a creature whenever Xira attacks. Then if a creature with one of the counters dies it causes an Insect creature token to be created. This represents Xira planting Insect eggs in another creature.

Alchemy: Dominaria brought the return of Egg counters on Darigaaz, Shivan Champion. Similar to their first appearance, they are created on a creature in exiled, then act as an upkeep tracker with one being removed each turn. In this instance, the counters are used to represent Darigaaz's ability to create a new Dragon brood.
Egg counter.use: Upkeep tracker; Creature token created when creature dies

Elixir counter.intro: Elixir counters are a type of counter introduced in Tempest. They act as a resource for a life gain ability.
Elixir counter.description: Elixir counters first appeared on Essence Bottle in Tempest. The artifact could add the essence counters to it and then could expend them via another ability for 2 life per counter.

Ember counter.intro: Ember counters are a type of counter introduced in Innistrad: Midnight Hunt. It acts as a counter for the Transform mechanic.
Ember counter.description: Ember counters first appeared on Smoldering Egg in Innistrad: Midnight Hunt. The creature would gain counters on it equal to the mana cost of any sorcery or instant cast by the player. Whenever the creature gains 7 or more counters, it transforms into Ashmouth Dragon. This represents the Egg absorbing mana from the spells until it hatches and transforms into the Dragon.

Energy counter.intro: Energy is a resource and mechanic that was introduced in the Kaladesh block (Kaladesh and Aether Revolt). The mechanic enables the production of energy counters, which may be used to pay the costs of activated and triggered abilities.
Energy counter.description: An energy counter is a counter that, unlike most other counters, is placed on players rather than objects. Most cards that grant energy counters also provide a way to spend them. However, because they are placed on the player rather than a specific object, energy counters from one card can be saved up and spent on the abilities of other cards. Energy counters don't go away as phases or steps end, or as the turn ends, and no cards printed in the Kaladesh block remove energy counters from other players. They could only be removed when the player chose to spend them. However, Core Set 2019 featured Suncleanser which could remove energy counters.

Enlightened counter.intro: Enlightened counters are a type of counter introduced in Dungeons & Dragons: Adventures in the Forgotten Realms. They act as a memory aid for an ability but on their own have no actual effect.
Enlightened counter.description:
Enlightened counters first appeared on The Book of Exalted Deeds in Dungeons & Dragons: Adventures in the Forgotten Realms. The legendary artifact has an ability which exiles itself and places an Enlightened counter on an angel. Alongside this, it also creates Angel creature tokens each turn if the player gained more than 3 life.

The ability that adds an Enlightened counter also gives the ability “You can’t lose the game and your opponents can’t win the game.” to the target angel. The creature keeps the ability even if it later stops being an angel or if the counter is removed. Transferring the counter to another creature does not grant the ability. The counters only serve as a memory aid to the player.

Eon counter.intro: Eon counters are a type of counter introduced in Zendikar. They act as a marker for a delayed time.
Eon counter.description:
Eon counters first appeared on Magosi, the Waterveil in Zendikar. It is a land with the ability to add eon counters to itself while skipping the player's next turn. It then has a second ability to remove the eon counter which gives the player an extra turn after their current one.

The counters returned for Out of the Tombs in the Warhammer 40,000 Commander Decks.

Eruption counter.intro: Eruption counters are a type of counter introduced in Doctor Who. They act as a counter for damage dealt to creatures and players when chaos ensues.
Eruption counter.description: Eruption counters first appeared on Pompeii in Doctor Who. They act as markers on the plane card with one being added whenever a blank is rolled on the planar die. Then whenever chaos ensues damage is dealt to each creature and player corresponding to the number of the eruption counters. This represents the pressure building up until the volcano explodes.
Eruption counter.use: Damage to all creatures and players when chaos ensues

Everything counter.intro: Everything counters are a type of counter introduced in Modern Horizons 3. It acts as a pseudo-Shapeshifter effect to mimic the abilities of Vesuvan shapeshifters.
Everything counter.description: Everything counters first appeared on Omo, Queen of Vesuva in Modern Horizons 3.
Everything counter.use: Creatures and Lands gain all of their respective subtypes.

Experience counter.intro: Experience counters are used to track a commander's growth in power throughout the game. They are only used on cards designed for multiplayer formats.
Experience counter.description:
Unlike most other counters, experience counters are placed on players, rather than on permanents. Experience counters first appeared through a cycle of commander in Commander 2015. Each legendary creature in the cycle has a triggered ability that grants its controller an experience counter, and a second ability that benefits from experience counters.

Because experience counters are put on players, they stay on you even if a commander dies, and said commander will reap the benefits the next time it's cast. Additionally, multiple cards in this cycle could accumulate counters in tandem, though naturally only one will benefit from the commander designation.

Exposure counter.intro: Exposure counters are a type of counter introduced in Doctor Who. They act as an Upkeep counter for rising "exposure" to "Byzantium Radiation," causing the active player to lose that much life.
Exposure counter.description: Exposure counters first appeared on Aplan Mortarium in Doctor Who. They act as markers on the plane card. With one being added to the plane during the active players upkeep, causing that player to lose an equivalent amount of life. This represents the exposure to radiation a player has experienced since planeswalking to the plane.

Eyeball counter.intro: Eyeball counters are a type of counter introduced in Dark Ascension and later reprinted in Commander 2013. It acts as a resource for a Tutor activated ability.
Eyeball counter.description: Eyeball counters first appeared on Jar of Eyeballs in Dark Ascension. Two eyeball counters were added to it whenever the player's creature died. An activated ability could then be used to remove the counters and choose a card from the top cards of the library equal to the number of counters while putting the rest at the bottom of the library. This represents using the creature's eyes to look at the top of the library.

Eyestalk counter.intro: Eyestalk counters are a type of counter introduced in the Mystery Booster on a playtest card.
Eyestalk counter.description: Eyestalk counters first appeared on Underdark Beholder playtest card in the Mystery Booster. It enters the battlefield with 10 of the counters on it. The counters act as a shield in that one is removed for each damage that would be dealt to the creature. If all are removed the creature is sacrificed. Whenever the creature attacked, it also lets the player reveal cards from the top of their library until an instant, sorcery, or enchantment with mana value less than the number of counters on it was found allowing it to be played without paying its mana cost. These counters represented the eyestalks of a Beholder.

Fade counter.intro: Fade counters are exclusively used by the fading mechanic.

Fate counter.intro: Fate counters are a type of counter introduced in Mirrodin. They act as a marker on a permanent for the use of another ability.
Fate counter.description: Fate counters first appeared on Oblivion Stone in Mirrodin and re-printed in various other sets. The artifact could add Fate counters to permanents and another to sacrifice itself destroying all permanents without Fate counters. The counter type re-appeared again on Triad of Fates in Theros where it could place Fate counters on creatures and other abilities to exile those creatures either temporarily or in exchange for drawing two cards. While there are no abilities gained or produced by fate counters, both cards use them as a way to "save" creatures marked. Triad of Fates is a cheap source of fate counters for the more impactful result of Oblivion Stone, while Oblivion Stone can let Triad of Fates protect itself with the second ability.
Fate counter.use: Marker on permanent for ability use

Feather counter.intro: Feather counters are a type of counter introduced in Invasion. They tend to grant bonuses or effects relating to birds.
Feather counter.description:
Feather counters first appeared on Kangee, Aerie Keeper in Invasion. It enters the battlefield with Feather counters on it if it was kicked. The counters grant +1/+1 to all birds on the battlefield. The counters appeared once again with the same effect in Judgment on Soulcatchers' Aerie which was an enchantment that gained a counter for every bird that is put into the player's graveyard.

In Alara Reborn, Feather counters returned with a different effect for Aven Mimeomancer. It would put a Feather counter on a creature each turn which gave the creature aspects of itself making it have a 3/1 base power and toughness and flying.

Feeding counter.intro: Feeding counters are a type of counter introduced in Foundations Jumpstart.
Feeding counter.description: The counters were first seen on Nazar, the Velvet Fang, a vampire warlock which gains the feeding counters in a representation of the amount of blood he drinks to revitalize himself. One of the counters is added to Nazar anytime the player gains life. Whenever he attacks, three of the counters may be removed in exchange for drawing three cards and losing three life.
Feeding counter.use: Drawing three cards in exchange for three life

Fellowship counter.intro: Fellowship counters are a type of counter introduced in Magic: The Gathering Foundations.
Fellowship counter.description: Banner of Kinship utilizes fellowship counters to show the size of the band marching under the banner. They allow the Banner to act as a Coat of Arms without the memory issues of tracking the effect's size.

Fetch counter.intro: Fetch counters are a type of counter introduced in Commander 2020. They are used as part of a partner ability that allows for exiled cards with the counter to be cast by the player.
Fetch counter.description:
Fetch counters first appeared on Pako, Arcane Retriever and Haldan, Avid Arcanist in Commander 2020. They are creatures with Partner for each other and have abilities that work with the counters. Whenever Pako attacks, the top card of each player's library is exiled with a Fetch counter on it. Pako gains a +1/+1 counter on it for each non-creature exiled that way. Haldan then can play cards that were exiled with fetch counters using mana of any color as the mana cost. The counters represent Halden's ability to fetch the cards Pako exiled.

Fetch counters were used in Alchemy: Eldraine by Hex, Kellan's Companion for similar purposes but utilizing the designed-for-digital mechanics.
Fetch counter.use: Marker on exiled cards that can be cast via an ability

Filibuster counter.intro: Filibuster counters are a type of counter introduced in Return to Ravnica. It acts as an upkeep counter for Alternate-win condition
Filibuster counter.description: Filibuster counters first appeared on Azor's Elocutors in Return to Ravnica. A Filibuster is put on the creature during each upkeep but one is also removed if the player takes damage. If it gains 5 Filibuster counters then the player wins the game. The name refers to the card trying to delay the opponent until victory can be achieved while the removal of damage represents the Filibuster getting interrupted.

Film counter.intro: Film counters are a type of counter introduced in Marvel's Spider-Man. They act as a resource to copy activated or triggered abilities.
Film counter.description: Film counters first appeared on Peter Parker's Camera. The camera enters with three film counters and its activated ability consumes one upon use.

Finality counter.intro: Finality counters are a type of deciduous counter introduced in The Lost Caverns of Ixalan. They were designed to minimize memory issues for cards that return something from the graveyard with "if it would die, it's exiled instead" rules.
Finality counter.description:
If a permanent with a finality counter on it would die, it is exiled instead. This is a replacement effect. The use of counters makes for better memory tracking, as permanents can be on the battlefield for long periods before their exiling is relevant. Having multiple finality counters on a permanent produces no additional effects.

This effect is usually used for creatures that have been returned from the graveyard to the battlefield at a reduced rate. Similar text was first seen as far back as Dreams of the Dead (Ice Age); later cards like Isareth, the Awakener or From the Catacombs sometimes used corpse counters to mark affected creatures. Unlike corpse counters, however, where the counter is merely a reminder and the ability remains regardless of the counter's presence, the rules for finality counters are included as part of the counter itself. Thus, if a finality counter is removed, upon destruction the creature returns to the graveyard as normal.

All colors have access to finality counters. Colors that bring things back from the graveyard are most likely to use it, with red, king of temporary effects, probably number one. In practice, however, black and its styles of reanimation has been first by a wide margin, followed by green, with red having only one representative of a {U}{B}{R} card.

Fire counter.intro: Fire counters are a type of counter introduced in Avatar: The Last Airbender. They are used to represent the additional power firebenders gain when Sozin's Comet passes by the world.

Flame counter.intro: Flame counters are a type of counter introduced in Planechase. Originally an upkeep tracker on a Plane, they've since been used as a resource for abilities on fire-related creatures.
Flame counter.description:
Flame counters first appeared on Naar Isle in Planechase. It was a plane card for Wildfire which used the counters as an Upkeep tracker to account for a rising amount of damage dealt to the player each turn. This represented the danger of being on this plane of fire.

They later appeared on a traditional card in Innistrad: Midnight Hunt with Embodiment of Flame. It would gain a Flame counter any time a spell the player controlled dealt damage. These Flame counters were then used as a resource for an activated ability to Exile the top card of the library while allowing it to be played during the turn.

They re-appeared again in three Magic: The Gathering Arena sets, first in Jumpstart: Historic Horizons on Managorger Phoenix, on Kardum, Patron of Flames in Alchemy Horizons: Baldur's Gate, and then Tend to the Kiln in Alchemy: Lorwyn. On Managorger Phoenix they represented its ability to reincarnate by giving it a counter Red mana cast during a spell. It would then return to the battlefield once it had 5 or more counters on it and also gained +1/+1 perpetually. On Kardum it gained a Flame counter every time it attacked while allowing the player to seek a card with the mana cost equal to the number of Flame counters. They would exile that card until Kardum died at which point all exiled cards would return to the player's hand for one turn after which they are discarded. Tend to the Kiln ties flame counters to the spiritual beliefs of Lorwyn's flamekin and their journey on the Path of Flame.

Flood counter.intro: Flood counters are a type of counter introduced in Mirrodin. They are usually related to water-themed effects.
Flood counter.description: Flood counters first appeared on Quicksilver Fountain in Mirrodin. It is an artifact that lets players put a flood counter on a non-island land, turning it into an Island. This represents land flooding. If all the lands on the battlefield become islands, then the artifact removes all the flood counters.

Foreshadow counter.intro: Foreshadow counters are a type of counter introduced in Ikoria: Lair of Behemoths. They buildup acting as a resource for an ability.
Foreshadow counter.description: Foreshadow counters first appeared on Ominous Seas in Ikoria: Lair of Behemoths. One of the counters is added to the enchantment every time the player draws a card. It then could remove 8 of the counters to create an 8/8 blue Kraken creature token. In this case, the counters foreshadow the appearance of the Kraken.

Fungus counter.intro: Fungus counters are a type of counter introduced in Mirage. They are a counter for creatures and have had two different effects with one use freezing the affected creature while another spawned saprolings on their death.
Fungus counter.description:
Fungus counters first appeared on Mindbender Spores in Mirage. It is a Wall which creates four Spore counters on creatures it blocks against. It freezes the creature preventing it from untapping while it has any counters on it but one counter being removed each upkeep step. This represents the fungus spreading on the creature from the wall.

They returned in Urza's Saga with Sporogenesis which was an enchantment that had a different effect for them. In this case, it added a fungus counter to a creature each upkeep and when any of those creatures die, a 1/1 green Saproling token would be created. These counters remained only until the enchantment left the battlefield. This effect represents the fungus's role in the decomposition of the dead.
Fungus counter.use: Freeze creature; Saproling created on creature death

Fury counter.intro: Fury counters are a type of counter introduced in Commander 2016. They build up if no creatures attack during a turn and also deal damage to the player.
Fury counter.description: Fury counters first appeared on Charging Cinderhorn in Commander 2016. It was a creature that would gain a Fury counter on any player's turn that doesn't attack and also deal damage to that player for however many Fury counters were on it. This represented the Ox becoming angrier anytime no one attacked and unleashing its fury on the player.
Fury counter.use: Deals damage to the player if no creatures attack during the turn

Fuse counter.intro: Fuse counters are a type of counter introduced in Weatherlight. They have acted as upkeep tracking for sacrificial and destructive abilities.
Fuse counter.description:
Fuse counters first appeared on Goblin Bomb in Weatherlight. It was an enchantment that would gain or lose a Fuse counter each upkeep based on a flipping a coin. It then had a sacrificial ability to remove 5 Fuse counters from it to deal 20 damage to the target Player or Planeswalker acting almost as an alternate-win condition since most often a player would not have more than 20 life.

They later appeared again in Urza's Destiny on Incendiary and Powder Keg. Incendiary was an aura enchantment that would gain a Fuse counter for each upkeep and then would deal damage to any target once the enchanted creature dies. Powder Keg also optionally gained a Fuse counter for each upkeep and had an activated sacrificial ability to destroy each artifact and creature with a mana value exactly equal to the number of counters.

In Odyssey the counters appeared on Bomb Squad which was a creature that had an activated ability to place Fuse counters on other creatures. A creature would then be destroyed once it had 4 or more Fuse counters on it deals 4 damage to its controller as well.

Gem counter.intro: Gem counter are a type of counter introduced in Khans of Tarkir. It acts as a resource on an artifact for an activated ability.
Gem counter.description: Gem counters first appeared on Briber's Purse in Khans of Tarkir. It enters the battlefield with a number of Gem counters equal to how much mana was paid to cast it. It then has an activated ability which can spend the Gem counters to prevent a creature from attacking or blocking for the rest of the turn.

Ghostform counter.intro: Ghostform counters are a type of counter introduced in Kaldheim. They are related to the planeswalker Kaya and act as a reminder for one of her loyalty abilities. It is named after Kaya's Ghostform, which had her name and has a similar effect.
Ghostform counter.description:
Ghostform counters first appeared on Kaya the Inexorable in Kaldheim. She has a Loyalty ability which adds a ghostform counter to a nontoken creature. The ability adds a counter and causes creatures to return it to their owner’s hand when they die or are put into exile along with a 1/1 white Spirit creature token with flying being created. This represents the creature returning to life as a spirit token.

The counter itself doesn’t have any functional importance and is just used to remind the player of the ability the creature gains. Even if that counter is removed from the creature, the triggered ability it gains will still work.

Glyph counter.intro: Glyph counters are a type of counter introduced in Legends. They temporarily freeze a creature for a turn per counter.
Glyph counter.description: Glyph counters first appeared on Glyph of Delusion in Legends as unnamed counters which were later given errata to Glyph counters. It is an instant which places counters equal to a given creature's toughness on it that was blocked by a Wall during the turn. They cause the creature to not untap during the turn with one counter being removed during the player's upkeep.
Glyph counter.use: Freezes creature; 1 counter removed each upkeep.

Gold counter.intro: Gold counters are a type of counter introduced in Onslaught. It has been used to turn creatures into Walls with Defender and later as a resource for an artifact's activated ability.
Gold counter.description: Gold counters first appeared on Aurification in Onslaught. It was an Enchantment that would cause Gold counters to be placed on creatures that deal damage to the player. They would transform those creatures into Walls with Defender preventing them from attacking. The counters are then removed once the enchantment leaves the battlefield. They reappeared again in Commander Legends: Battle for Baldur's Gate on Dragon's Hoard. It is an artifact which spawns a Gold counter on it whenever a Dragon enters the battlefield and can then spend them on an activated ability for drawing a card. The two types of Gold counters currently do not currently interact with each other at all.
Gold counter.use: Turns creatures into Walls with Defender; Resource

Growth counter.intro: Growth counters are a type of counter introduced in Mirage. They have thus far been always tied to enchantments and represent some form of increasing effect each turn.
Growth counter.description:
Growth counters first appeared on Malignant Growth in Mirage. It is an enchantment which gains a Growth counter every upkeep. It then allows all opponents to draw a card for each counter while also taking damage for each. The counters appeared once again in Urza's Destiny for Momentum which was an aura enchantment which added a new Growth counter each upkeep while giving the creature +1/+1 for each.

They eventually re-appeared in Ravnica Allegiance on Simic Ascendancy which was an enchantment that had growth counters put on it whenever a +1/+1 counter was put on a creature. It also had an activated ability to create +1/+1 counters. It had an alternate-win condition once 20 or more Growth counters were on it.

The most recent usage of Growth counters appeared on Paradox Zone in Commander 2021. It was an enchantment that entered the battlefield with 1 counter. On the player's end step, the number of tokens would double and it would then create a green/blue Fractal creature token which got +1/+1 for each Growth counter on the enchantment.

Hack counter.intro: Hack counters are a type of counter introduced in Unfinity. They act as a resource for an activated ability.
Hack counter.description: Hack counters first appeared on Truss, Chief Engineer in Unfinity. One of the Hack counters is placed on it when it enters the battlefield and whenever another creature dies. Truss then has an activated ability that allows for the removal of X Hack counters in exchange for adding or subtracting X from a number or word on the target spell or permanent until the end of the turn without reducing a number below 1 or a number word below one. This represents the ability to hack the spell or the permanent.

Harmony counter.intro: Harmony counters are a type of counter introduced in Dungeons & Dragons: Adventures in the Forgotten Realms. They act as an upkeep tracker allowing higher mana cost creatures to be searched for as more turns pass.
Harmony counter.description: Harmony counter first appeared on Instrument of the Bards in Dungeons & Dragons: Adventures in the Forgotten Realms. One of the Harmony counters is placed on the artifact on each upkeep. It then has an activated ability that allows the player to search their library for a creature with a mana value equal to the number of the counters on it and place that in their hand. If the creature is legendary, it also creatures a Treasure token. The counters represent the harmony of the song increasing each turn the longer the instrument is played making it able to call forth more powerful creatures.

Hatching counter.intro: Hatching counters are a type of counter introduced in Kamigawa: Neon Dynasty.
Hatching counter.description: Hatching counters first appeared on The Dragon-Kami Reborn in Kamigawa: Neon Dynasty. It is a saga enchantment that for its first two lore counter abilities it will let the player look at the top 3 cards of their library and exile 1 of them face down with one of the counters on it while putting the other 2 at the bottom of the library. Its third lore counter ability transforms it into Dragon-Kami's Egg which can cast a spell from the exiled cards with Hatching counters without paying its mana cost whenever it or another Dragon dies.
Hatching counter.use: Cast marked spell from exile on a Dragon's death

Hatchling counter.intro: Hatchling counters are a type of counter introduced in Legends. They have represented creatures hatching from an egg via the ability and the transform mechanic.
Hatchling counter.description:
Hatchling counters first appeared on Triassic Egg in Legends where they originally appeared as unnamed counters before being given errata into Hatchling counters. It was an artifact with an activated ability to add Hatchling counters to it and which could then be sacrificed once two or more counters are on it. The sacrifice then allows the player to either move a creature from the player's hand or graveyard to the battlefield. This represents the creature hatching from the egg.

The counters returned on Ludevic's Test Subject in Innistrad where it acted as a counter for the transform mechanic. It had an ability to put the Hatchling counters on it until 5 of them triggers the transformation from a Lizard Egg to Ludevic's Abomination, a Lizard Horror.
Hatchling counter.use: Resource for sacrificial ability; Transform tracking

Healing counter.intro: Healing counters are a type of counter introduced in Ice Age. They have been associated with a Fylgja and have been used to prevent damage from being dealt to a creature.
Healing counter.description:
Healing counters first appeared on Fylgja in Ice Age. It is an Aura enchantment that can be placed on a creature. It enters into play with 4 healing counters though more can be added via an activated ability. It then has another ability to prevent 1 damage to the enchanted creature in exchange for a healing counter.

The counters appeared once again in Coldsnap on Ursine Fylgja which is a creature that also comes into play with 4 of the counters on it with its activated ability to add more. It then has a similar ability to remove a counter to prevent the next 1 damage that would be dealt to the creature during the turn.

Hit counter.intro: Hit counters are a type of counter introduced in Guilds of Ravnica. They have been related to Assassins marking cards that get exiled and which can be counted for a future effect.
Hit counter.description:
Hit counters first appeared on Etrata, the Silencer in Guilds of Ravnica. Whenever she dealt damage to a player, she would exile one of their creatures with a Hit counter on it. The player would then lose the game if they had 3 or more exiled cards with Hit counters on them. This represented the assassin killing the player.

The counters returned in New Capenna Commander on Mari, the Killing Quill which would exile and put a Hit counter on any opponent creature that dies. It then gave Assassins, Mercenaries, and Rogues the ability to remove a Hit counter whenever they dealt damage to the player and gain a card and two Treasure tokens. Ravenloft Adventurer from Commander Legends: Battle for Baldur's Gate had a similar effect of exiling an opponent's creatures with a Hit counter when they died. In this, the player needs to complete a Dungeon which would cause the opponent to lose 1 life for each exiled card with a Hit counter whenever the creature attacks.
Hit counter.use: Assassins marking exiled cards for future effect

Hope counter.intro: Hope counters are a type of counter introduced in The Lord of the Rings: Tales of Middle-Earth.
Hope counter.description: Hope counters first appeared on Dawn of a New Age to track the number of cards that may be drawn. They represent the growing hope of a peaceful new age after the War of the Ring.

Hone counter.intro: Hone counters are a type of counter introduced in Strixhaven: School of Mages. They act as an upkeep tracker on exiled instants and sorceries that can be cast with a lesser mana cost after a few turns.
Hone counter.description: Hone counters first appeared on Uvilda, Dean of Perfection in Strixhaven: School of Mages. The creature has an activated ability to exile an instant or sorcery card from the player's hand with three hone counters on it. One of the counters is then removed on each upkeep and after every counter is removed, the player may cast the spell for less mana. This represents the player taking time to hone their skill with the spell.
Hone counter.use: Upkeep tracking for casting exiled instant or sorcery with less mana cost

Hoofprint counter.intro: Hoofprint counter are a type of counter introduced in Lorwyn. They act as a resource for an enchantment's ability.
Hoofprint counter.description: Hoofprint counters first appeared on Hoofprints of the Stag in Lorwyn. It has since been reprinted in various Commander decks as well including Commander 2016, Commander 2020, and New Capenna Commander. It is an enchantment that has a Hoofprint counter placed on each time a card is drawn by the player. The counters then act as an additional resource for an ability to create a Flying Elemental creature token by removing 4 of the counters from it.

Hour counter.intro: Hour counters are a type of counter introduced in Kaladesh. They are used on cards to count down or count up for some effect.
Hour counter.description:
Hour counters first appeared on Midnight Oil in Kaladesh. It is an enchantment that enters the battlefield with 7 Hour counters limiting the player's maximum hand size to the number of counters while penalizing discarding via lost life. At each draw step, it allows for the drawing of an additional card while two hour counters are removed from it.

They appeared once again in Throne of Eldraine on Midnight Clock with a different usage. This time the artifact gained an hour counter on each upkeep building up to 12 while having the ability to add additional ones for some mana. When it hit 12, the player would shuffle their hand and graveyard into their library and draw a new hand. Rusko, Clockmaker from Alchemy: The Brothers' War later became the first creature to use hour counters with it directly adding the counters to all Midnight Clocks under the players control whenever the player cast a non-creature spell.

Hour counters appeared on the 2024 Las Vegas Unknown Event playtest card The Bus Runner which creates a token with 8 of the counters on it with one being removed whenever the token or a gamer is tapped. Once all are removed, the player gains a life while opponents lose a life. Then 8 more counters re re-added. This represents a countdown on the card.
Hour counter.use: Count up or down for effect

Hourglass counter.intro: Hourglass counters are a type of counter introduced in Invasion. They prevent the untapping of creatures and lands during the unstap step.
Hourglass counter.description: Hourglass counters first appeared on Temporal Distortion in Invasion. It was an enchantment that added Hourglass counters on any land or creature that became tapped. The counter would then prevent them from untapping during the untap step. However, all the Hourglass counters on a specific player's permanents would then get removed on the player's upkeep step.
Hourglass counter.use: Prevents untapping during the untap step

Hunger counter.intro: Hunger counters are a type of counter introduced in The Dark. They act as an upkeep counter for an enchantment related to the skipping of drawing cards.
Hunger counter.description: Hunger counters first appeared on Fasting in The Dark as unnamed counters, which were later renamed Hunger counters. The counters act as an upkeep tracker on the enchantment, causing it to be destroyed once 5 counters are on it. This represents the end of fasting due to built-up hunger. The Hunger is the skipping of drawing cards as the enchantments get destroyed if any card is drawn. In exchange, it gives life to the player each turn.

Ice counter.intro: Ice counters are a type of counter introduced in Ice Age. They are usually related to ice or snow-themed effects.
Ice counter.description:
Ice counters first appeared on Iceberg in Ice Age. It would enter the battlefield with X on it for however much extra mana is paid to cast it. could be paid to add additional ones while 1 counter could be removed in exchange for .

Coldsnap saw the return of the counter on several cards with varying effects. Rimefeather Owl could add snow counters to a target permanent which causes them to gain the Snow attribute. Dark Depths enters the battlefield with 10 ice counters on it and then could remove a counter for . Once all are removed, it is sacrificed causing a 20/20 black Avatar creature token with flying and indestructible to be created. Rimescale Dragon can tap a creature and add an ice counter to it which freezes it causing it to not untap as long as the counter is on it. The final usage in Coldsnap was on Woolly Razorback which enters the battlefield with 3 of the counters on it. While on it, the creature cannot deal damage and has defender with one being removed every time it blocks.

The counters re-appeared on Thing in the Ice in Shadows over Innistrad as a counter for transforming. It enters the battlefield with 4 ice counters on it and transforms into Awoken Horror when they are removed with one being removed for each instant or sorcery being cast.

In Kaldheim they appeared on Draugr Necromancer which exiles an opponent's creatures that die with a ice counter on it. The player can then cast exiled cards an opponent owns with ice counters on them with mana from snow sources available to be used as the mana of any color.

Impostor counter.intro: Impostor counters are a type of counter introduced in Murders at Karlov Manor.
Impostor counter.description: Impostor counters are used as a thematic representation of creatures in disguise that doesn't use the set's Cloak or Disguise mechanics. Illicit Masquerade allows creatures with imposter counters to be swapped with creatures in your graveyard as they die.

Incarnation counter.intro: Incarnation counters are a type of counter introduced in Core Set 2021. They act as a replacement for player damage which leads to an alternate loss condition.
Incarnation counter.description: Incarnation counters first appeared on Nine Lives in Core Set 2021. It is an enchantment that prevents damage from being done to the player in exchange for adding an Incarnation counter to it. If the number of counters reaches nine then the enchantment is exiled. If the enchantment leaves the battlefield, the player loses the game. This represents the common saying that a cat has nine lives with each counter representing an incarnation or life of the player.
Incarnation counter.use: Replacement of player damage for alternate loss condition

Infection counter.intro: Infection counters are a type of counter introduced in Alliances.
Infection counter.description: Infection counters first appeared on Diseased Vermin in Alliances. They are created on the creature whenever it deals damage to an enemy player. Damage would then be dealt to a target opponent based on how many infection counters are on the creature at each upkeep.
